summary: Research and design a Bitcoin L2 over Nostr relays intended to succeed Lightning
logs: Winner: design A (Federated-Ark over Nostr); votes {"A":2,"C":1}; 15 grafts, 3 flaws flagged on winner
Attack panel done: 42 attacks (9 critical, 21 high)

judges.rationale: A's trust claims survive adversarial walking: I tried to break the arkoor contest (stale sender exit vs receiver keyspend inside the 144-CSV window) and it resolves trustlessly to the rightful owner; exits are fully pre-signed, quantified to the vB, and need no operator. Its nonce/session discipline over lossy relays is best-in-class, and it alone flags FROST-inside-MuSig2 as unproven. B is a close, sound second — receiver-online claim makes its key-tweak math actually work, and locktime ordering is consensus-enforced — but suffers 4-week exit maturity, change-desk dependence per payment, and a 36-block stale-race under mass exit. C's core mechanisms break: the send-time share-tweak to an offline receiver's independent key is cryptographically impossible (no party knows the scalar u_k−u_{k+1}), and the federation alone can steal any transferred leaf via stale-exit + public forfeit that pays the federation. Exit data also load-bears on Blossom HTTP, violating R2.

Economics/UX lens. A is the most trust-minimized but its two-sided economics are adoption-fatal: refresh fees pass through operator cost-of-capital on the user's whole balance (~0.4%/mo, ~5%/yr carrying cost), idle wallets get force-exited on-chain at the user's expense after ~25 days, and operators tie up 10 BTC per 10k users to earn roughly their cost of capital. B has the best consumer-money properties (seed-only consensus recovery, zero-cost dormancy, simplest receiver path) but amortizes nothing on-chain — one permanent UTXO per coin is Lightning-parity footprint, not a successor. C engineers the economics deliberately: payments don't consume operator capital (~10% float), user carrying cost near zero, healthy operator margin, LSP-pivot migration, offline receive including offline LN invoices. A and C tie on points; under a fees-and-business-model lens C wins the tiebreak. A normal user would plausibly pick C over an LSP; only C and B beat Cashu's hold-for-free property.

Lens: decentralization/censorship resistance. A has the hardest trust floor: checkpointed funds are theft-proof even under full quorum collusion (the user co-signed and key-deleted their own path), so capture degrades to censorship, and censorship degrades to a safe unilateral exit; a dead quorum cannot even sweep. Cross-pool vHTLC federation gives a mesh-of-small-federations answer to LN's hub convergence; towers are permissionless and defenses pay users directly, not the operator. B behaves best under quorum death (consensus-ordered locktimes, true seed-only recovery leaf, dormancy degrades to plain self-custody) but per-coin UTXO scaling breaks the successor mandate, and a 4-week premeditated-retention theft window remains. C is the most capital-efficient (lowest operator entry barrier) but its stale-exit defense is a mempool race whose remedy pays the federation — uncleansed receivers lose operator-independent exit precisely when the quorum fails. A's residual costs: capital-concentration pressure, DA-dependent seed recovery.

winnerFlaws.flaw: Every signature in the system depends on a FROST group acting as one MuSig2 cosigner (threshold generation of MuSig2's two-point nonces and binding-factor partials). No proven, shipped construction exists; FROSTR/bifrost only does plain Schnorr over Nostr. The design flags it with an audit gate, but if the composition leaks nonces or keys, the whole pool is compromised. Related: the hash-locked forfeit/new-leaf atomicity is asserted, not specified at script level.

Structural Ark carrying cost: operators front full vTXO value for 30-day expiries, so users pay ~0.4%/month (~5%/yr) on their entire balance just to hold, and any wallet idle >~25 days is force-exited on-chain (4.5k-22k sats) at the user's expense. Combined with operator revenue (~0.4-0.5%/mo) barely covering the stated 5% APY cost of 10 BTC/10k-user float, both sides of the market are unviable versus Cashu or LSP-Lightning for normal users.

Load-bearing liveness assumption: hourly interactive MuSig2 tree ceremonies with up to ~1024 cosigners must complete two signing rounds over untrusted, lossy public relays within 30-second phase timers. Persistent ceremony failure (relay drops/latency at scale) cascades users into trust-downgraded delegated refreshes or forced on-chain exits — the protocol's safety degrades through its own retry path.

grafts.idea: Seed-only recovery leaf: a per-output script path paying the checkpointed owner after epoch_end+288 CLTV, rotated at each refresh — gives A full recovery with zero stored data even if all relays purge the vault and all operators die.

Consensus-enforced staleness ordering via decrementing absolute locktimes on pre-signed exit txs — layering this onto A's arkoor chains would make stale-exit defense proactive-by-consensus instead of depending on someone broadcasting within the 144-block CSV contest window.
Per-operator signed deletion attestations and epoch heartbeat events (kind 31401): cheap public accountability making share retention provable fraud after the fact.

Merkle-rooted leaf-ownership state commitments with strictly increasing sequence numbers (kind 30178): compact inclusion proofs for receivers and portable equivocation fraud proofs, stronger than A's flat per-vTXO sequence log.
Watchtower 'broadcast-exit-at-height-H unless superseded' pre-deposits — closes A's gap where a never-yet-online arkoor receiver has no watch request filed before T_exp.

Wallet-enforced value-at-risk cap with automatic checkpoint participation above a threshold (default ~50k sats) — turns A's 'uncheckpointed balance displayed distinctly' into a bounded-exposure policy.

Consensus-level recovery tapleaf: rotate a CLTV-gated recovery leaf to the current owner at each checkpoint so full recovery from seed alone works even if relays, Blossom, and all operators vanish — eliminates C's data-availability doomsday and is the single best consumer-trust property in any design.

Decrementing absolute-locktime staleness ordering on exit txs, making stale exits consensus-invalid until the rightful owner's matures. This replaces C's 72-block forfeit race (and its forfeit-pays-Fed IOU gap) with 'act before a known deadline' — no mempool race, no watchtower-dependence for ordering.

Zero-cost dormancy: untransferred/unmoved value skips rollover entirely — no carrying fee, no liveness requirement, no forced exit for idle users. Grafting an idle-leaf path (long-lived ladder rungs + recovery tapleaf) into C removes the 'open the app monthly or get force-exited' one-star-review generator.

Recovery-leaf script path (rotating <owner> CHECKSIG + CLTV fallback): gives true seed-only recovery with zero data-availability assumptions and means dormant funds degrade to plain self-custody instead of being swept at T_exp. A's seed recovery currently fails if all 8 relays AND 5 operators withhold vault ciphertext, and dormant tower-less users are confiscated by the expiry sweep.

Decrementing absolute-locktime ordering on successive exit/claim packages, so the rightful current owner's exit is consensus-valid strictly before any stale one — replaces A's 144-CSV reactive contest (which needs a watchtower or receiver awake within 24h) with deadline-based, race-free defense.

Per-operator signed deletion attestations published per epoch (kind 31401): cheap public accountability that converts share/key retention into provable fraud after the fact — directly applicable to A's ephemeral tree-signing keys and FROST share refreshes.

Receiver-side replication-verified finality: don't display a received payment as final until the transfer package is confirmed replicated on >=k independent relays/mirrors. Detects relay withholding at receive time instead of at recovery time.

Watchtower height-deposits ('broadcast this pre-signed exit at height H unless superseded'): makes offline-past-deadline safety automatic and fee-budgeted rather than dependent on towers noticing missed-heartbeat alerts in A's thin watch-request market.

LSP migration framing plus offline BOLT11 receive via federation-held preimage shards (Spark-precedented): strengthens A's R1/R8 story — existing Lightning LSPs pivot to pool operators with the same capital and no per-edge lockup, and npubs can receive native Lightning invoices while offline.

attacks.name: Deterministic secnonce reuse extracts private keys / FROST shares (whole-pool theft)
attacks.description: The load-bearing nonce rule derives secnonce=H(round-id‖attempt‖signer-set‖tx-digest), omitting counterparties' pubnonces. MuSig2 forces committing your nonce before seeing others', so deterministic nonces are provably unsafe (the reason MuSig-DN exists). Attack: a malicious co-signer/relay sends a proposal for one session-id with nonce-set N1; victim signs s1=k+e1·a·x and 'deletes' k. Relay drops s1 and induces a crash or same-attempt retry; the victim re-derives the identical k, now against nonce-set N2 (aggregate nonce differs, giving e2). Two partials, same k, e1≠e2 yield x=(s1−s2)/(e1−e2). This recovers a user key or an operator FROST share; collect k shares, reconstruct Q, drain the entire pool.
attacks.mitigation: Never use deterministic nonces in MuSig2/FROST round 1. Use CSPRNG nonces plus a durable monotonic anti-reuse log (BIP-327 secnonce hygiene), or MuSig-DN's ZK-proven derivation. Abort permanently if any session-id repeats and forbid post-crash re-signing of an attempt unless a persisted used-nonce record proves the partial was never emitted.
attacks.residualRisk: Durable used-nonce logs conflict with the stateless, seed-only wallet goal; a wiped or restored device can still be induced to reuse a nonce.

attacks.name: FROST-threshold-of-MuSig2 composition leaks the group key under split relay view
attacks.description: Q signs as one MuSig2 cosigner whose two nonce points and binding-factor partial are FROST-threshold-generated — no shipped, proven construction exists (FROSTR does plain Schnorr only). MuSig2's binding factor b=H(aggnonce,msg) depends on the user's nonces. Over untrusted relays the coordinator/user splits the view: deliver nonce-set N to operator O1 and N' to O2 inside one session. Operators compute different b, produce FROST partials over inconsistent challenges; Lagrange-combining inconsistent partials yields a signature whose algebra leaks the group secret or is forgeable (Drijvers/ROS-class). Open many concurrent ≤1024-cosigner sessions (lossy relays guarantee aborts/retries) to grind candidates. One success compromises Q = total pool theft.
attacks.mitigation: Treat as unshipped crypto behind a formal-proof and external-audit gate before mainnet (the design flags this). Operators must canonicalize and sign the full session transcript (every pubnonce, signer set, message) and verify identical views before emitting any partial; abort on any divergence; strictly bound concurrent open sessions per group key.
attacks.residualRisk: Even with transcript checks the composition is unproven; one subtle leak in the threshold binding-factor computation compromises every signature Q ever produces.

attacks.name: Arkoor double-spend with eclipsed 38403 detection and unactionable fraud proof
attacks.description: Arkoor double-spend needs sender U plus 3-of-5 Q (admitted), but the claimed net — receiver checks 38403 on ≥3 relays and gets a no-conflict attestation — fails because R2 lets relays selectively serve. Colluding Q cosigns U's leaf to Bob (seq=n) and publishes it only to relays the attacker controls for Bob's npub, while a conflicting spend back to U goes to other relays. Bob, eclipsed on his NIP-65 read relays, sees only the 'paid' entry and ships goods. Bob's later refresh is rejected (leaf already spent). The 'portable fraud proof' is worthless: FROST shares carry no on-chain bond, so a smash-and-grab's gain dwarfs reputational cost. The bounded trust window is really uncapped custodial loss.
attacks.mitigation: Receiver must fetch 38403 from disjoint relay sets including its own relays and fail closed on any absence/timeout, and confirm replication on ≥k independent mirrors before treating funds as spendable. Bond operators with on-chain collateral slashable by the equivocation proof; absent bonded slashing, hard-cap uncheckpointed receive value.
attacks.residualRisk: Fail-closed receive reintroduces withholding DoS; a globally eclipsing adversary still blinds the receiver; bonding needs operator capital the federation may not post.

attacks.name: Forfeit/new-leaf hash-lock atomicity break enables refresh theft and mass forfeit
attacks.description: Refresh atomicity rests on a Bark-style hash-lock: the old-leaf forfeit and the new leaf both gate on preimage X that Q reveals 'after the new round tx confirms' — asserted, not script-bound. If X is not cryptographically bound to the specific round tx containing the user's new leaf, colluding Q can confirm a round tx that omits or relocates the victim's new leaf, then reveal X (legitimately for included users), broadcast the victim's forfeit, and sweep the old leaf — victim loses the vTXO and gets no replacement. Worse, if one shared preimage gates many forfeits, revealing it for the included users simultaneously unlocks the forfeits of excluded users, enabling mass refresh theft in a single round.
attacks.mitigation: Specify atomicity at script level: make the forfeit's spend condition derivable only from the confirmed round txid that actually includes the user's leaf (e.g., a per-user preimage committed inside that leaf), so the forfeit is unspendable unless the matching new leaf exists on-chain. Use distinct per-user preimages, never a shared round preimage.
attacks.residualRisk: Covenant-less Bitcoin cannot truly bind a pre-signed forfeit to another transaction's confirmation; any construction leaves a window where Q controls reveal ordering.

attacks.name: Dead-quorum makes stale exits uncontestable, robbing arkoor recipients
attacks.description: The design claims a dead quorum (≥3 operators gone) is safe — 'theft impossible, coins go only to exiting users.' False for arkoor. The forfeit that punishes a stale exit spends the MuSig2(U,Q) keypath, requiring a LIVE Q partial. With Q dead, no forfeit can be produced. Attack: U sells a vTXO via arkoor (receives goods/cash off-chain), then waits for or induces quorum death (only three operators must be gone), and unilaterally exits the pre-sale leaf U still holds path/claim for. No forfeit is possible; the stale exit confirms after CSV; U double-spends and the buyer is robbed with zero recourse. Quorum liveness is therefore a theft-prevention dependency, not merely a payment-availability one.
attacks.mitigation: Make stale-exit defense consensus-enforced rather than Q-dependent via decrementing absolute-locktime ordering (design B) so the current owner's exit is valid strictly before any prior owner's — but that requires the buyer to hold a pre-signed exit, contradicting offline/keyless receive. Otherwise forbid any onward spend of received value until it is checkpointed.
attacks.residualRisk: Decrementing-locktime ordering is future-work and hard with covenant-less Ark; until shipped, all uncheckpointed arkoor is stealable whenever the quorum stalls or dies.

attacks.name: Delegated offline refresh lets the quorum re-sign a sock-puppet branch and steal the balance
attacks.description: In delegated offline refresh the user is not in the ceremony and signs nothing, so the new tree's internal keys = MuSig2-agg(co-branch users + Q) with no contribution the offline user can delete. Q both runs the refresh AND composes the branches. Attack: Q (3-of-5 colluding) places the delegated user's leaf in a subtree whose every other leaf is Q-controlled sock-puppet, and Q retains all ephemeral keys (deletion is unenforced; attestations are future-work). With all co-branch cosigners + Q under one party and zero honest deleters, the attacker re-signs the parent node to an alternate child redirecting the entire subtree to itself before the user returns (up to ~8 weeks). The design mis-frames this as a 'weaker covenant'; it is full-balance theft under the same collusion threshold.
attacks.mitigation: Disallow delegated refresh (default to watchtower exit), or require the offline user's pre-authorized key to be a mandatory cosigner of every new ancestor node so their deletion still gates it, with user-attested diverse co-branch composition. Ship kind-31401 signed deletion attestations as a hard precondition, not future work.
attacks.residualRisk: A user cannot delete a key they never generated; any delegated construction without the user as a deleting cosigner leaves Q+branch able to re-sign, and 'deletion' is fundamentally unprovable.

attacks.name: Refresh censorship plus watchtower suppression yields a confiscating T_exp sweep
attacks.description: Operators can steal from offline users by attrition without breaking crypto. Target a user whose refresh is due. Q stalls or refuses their refresh ceremony (censorship — an admitted capability) and, via the ≥2 operator-run paid relays in the pool's ≥8-relay set, withholds the target's kind-38404 watch request and kind-38405 alerts from the thin, operator-backstopped watchtower market; public relays are AUTH-gated/spammed for the target. The offline user's pre-signed exit never reaches a tower. At T_exp the quorum executes the 'legitimate' sweep (`<T_exp> CLTV <Q>`) and confiscates the funds. Censorship plus a thin watch market becomes outright confiscation of exactly the offline users R3 promises to protect.
attacks.mitigation: Diversify watch requests across many independent non-operator towers using design-C 'broadcast-at-height-H unless superseded' pre-deposits so action is automatic and fee-budgeted. Add the consensus recovery-tapleaf so dormant funds degrade to self-custody instead of being sweepable. Require multi-relay non-operator publication receipts before each refresh deadline.
attacks.residualRisk: The permissionless tower market is thin and unpaid; recovery-tapleaf is future-work; a resourced adversary can still degrade enough relays/towers to win some T_exp races.

attacks.name: 144-block forfeit race lost via TRUC/P2A pinning or replacement cycling (seller reclaims sold vTXO)
attacks.description: Unilateral exits are TRUC/v3 zero-fee with a P2A anchor CPFP'd by anyone. A seller who arkoor-sold a vTXO exits the pre-sale leaf; Q must broadcast the forfeit and CPFP it within the 144-block (~24h) CSV window. Because both forfeit and exit are zero-fee and depend on third-party CPFP, the attacker can win the fee race or run replacement-cycling on the shared anchor/child to evict or delay the forfeit's CPFP package until 144 blocks elapse, after which the stale exit claim matures and confirms. TRUC limits but does not eliminate cycling when an honest party must repeatedly re-fund a competing package. Net result: the seller double-spends the sold coin and the buyer is robbed. The decrementing-locktime fix is explicitly future-work.
attacks.mitigation: Adopt deadline-based decrementing-absolute-locktime ordering so the current owner's claim is consensus-valid before any stale one, removing the mempool race. Until then lengthen the contest window, mandate well-funded operator CPFP with pre-committed fee budgets, monitor for cycling, aggressively rebroadcast forfeits, and keep TRUC topology strictly 1p1c.
attacks.residualRisk: Replacement cycling has no complete mempool-policy fix; a miner-colluding or well-capitalized attacker can still delay forfeits across 144 blocks during fee spikes.

attacks.name: PTLC/vHTLC adaptor-secret leak via nonce reuse and swap replacement cycling
attacks.description: Cross-pool and LN bridging use vHTLC/PTLC adaptor signatures over MuSig2 between quorums. Adaptor sigs are maximally nonce-sensitive: the adaptor secret (the PTLC point's discrete log = payment secret) leaks if the underlying nonce repeats or if one adaptor is finalized against two contexts — exactly what the deterministic-secnonce rule (#1) plus relay-driven retries enable. Attack: induce a retry so a forwarding node finalizes two adaptor sigs under one nonce, extract the adaptor secret, then pull the incoming payment without revealing the preimage downstream, or claim the swap without paying. Separately, the admitted replacement-cycling exposure on the swap's 144-block CLTV lets an attacker cycle out the timeout claim and steal the swap output.
attacks.mitigation: Use fresh, anti-reuse-logged nonces for all adaptor/PTLC signing (never the deterministic session-id scheme); verify the adaptor point and recomputed challenge before finalizing; allow one finalize per nonce, durably recorded. For swaps, use conservative CLTV deltas, watchtower-backed rebroadcast, and treat cycling as a live threat (per the design's own admission).
attacks.residualRisk: Adaptor-secret leakage is catastrophic and silent; HTLC-path cycling remains unsolved at mempool level, so bridge liquidity stays at risk during congestion.

attacks.name: Long-offline arkoor receiver confiscated at T_exp (no watch request filed)
attacks.description: An arkoor receiver who never comes online before T_exp has no kind-38404 watch request filed (the design admits this gap). The funds sit at a leaf only that recipient's key controls, but since the recipient never acts, no exit is ever broadcast. At T_exp the quorum's legitimate sweep `<T_exp> CLTV <Q>` confiscates the coin. A motivated quorum mines its own 38403 log and gift-wrap archive to identify P_B recipients with no subsequent refresh or exit activity (long-dormant npubs), then simply waits out their clocks and sweeps. This is targeted theft of precisely the users R3/R4 promise to protect: receive while offline, zero prior setup.
attacks.mitigation: Ship design-C watchtower height-deposits ('broadcast pre-signed exit at H unless superseded') created at receive time by the sender on the receiver's behalf, plus the consensus recovery-tapleaf so dormant value degrades to self-custody rather than being swept. Make a funded watch request a mandatory part of every arkoor send.
attacks.residualRisk: Sender-filed watch requests can be withheld by relays (#7); recovery-tapleaf is future-work; truly never-online npubs still depend entirely on third parties acting in time.

attacks.name: Round-assembly view-split commits a victim's input to an aggregate key they cannot exit
attacks.description: The round-tx root internal key = MuSig2-agg(all ≤1024 participants' ephemeral keys, Q), assembled by Q over untrusted relays. Key-aggregation coefficients stop classic rogue-key cancellation only if every signer agrees on the exact participant set. Q splits the view: it shows victim U a participant set/tree (24401) in which U's leaf appears, collects U's partial over the root, but assembles the ACTUAL on-chain root from a different set/coefficients where U's value funds an output U cannot unilaterally exit (path differs from what U verified). Combined with the unbound forfeit hash-lock (#4), U releases its boarding/refresh input before confirming the real output matches, and Q captures the input at conversion.
attacks.mitigation: Before releasing any forfeit or boarding spend, every signer must verify that the FINAL aggregate key and confirmed round-tx output script exactly equal locally recomputed values from the signed participant set, and that their leaf and full path are present on-chain. Sign a canonical participant-set commitment; abort on mismatch; bind input release to confirmed-output verification.
attacks.residualRisk: Verification needs a reliable L1 view; an eclipsed or SPV-light signer can be shown false confirmations, re-enabling capture at conversion time.

attacks.name: Recovery-tapleaf graft names the stale pre-arkoor owner between checkpoints
attacks.description: The grafted seed-only recovery tapleaf pays the 'checkpointed owner after epoch_end+288 CLTV,' rotated only at each refresh/checkpoint — not at each arkoor hop. But arkoor transfers ownership off-chain between checkpoints, so after Alice arkoor-pays Bob the on-chain leaf's recovery path still names ALICE until the next refresh. Attack: Alice pays Bob; Bob holds uncheckpointed value; Alice (or anyone holding the prior recovery key) waits epoch_end+288 and sweeps the output via the stale recovery path, stealing Bob's received funds. The very graft sold as 'the single best consumer-trust property' reintroduces a stale-state theft window precisely for uncheckpointed arkoor — the funds Flock is already weakest on.
attacks.mitigation: Forbid onward arkoor spends of a leaf until its recovery tapleaf is rotated to the new owner (require a checkpoint before the recovery path can name a new owner), or make the recovery path's locktime strictly later than any outstanding arkoor claim. Rotate the recovery leaf atomically with each transfer, not only at refresh.
attacks.residualRisk: Atomic per-transfer rotation needs an on-chain or quorum action per hop, breaking the offline/zero-setup receive promise; otherwise the stale-owner window persists between checkpoints.

attacks.name: FROST proactive resharing/DKG over untrusted relays enables share corruption or recovery
attacks.description: FROST monthly proactive share refresh and the genesis PedPoP DKG run as kind-24404 messages over untrusted relays. Resharing is split-view-sensitive: a relay/coordinator that selectively drops or reorders reshare shares can drive operators to inconsistent share sets (bricking the group and forcing a mass exit), or by replaying old-epoch reshare messages alongside new ones induce an operator to combine cross-epoch material that aids reconstruction by the mobile adversary proactive refresh is meant to defeat. Over successive months an attacker who compromises different operator subsets each epoch can, without consistent transport authentication, accumulate enough to reconstruct the group key.
attacks.mitigation: Run DKG/resharing over authenticated, ordered, acknowledged channels with epoch-tagged transcripts and explicit complaint rounds; require all participants to sign and verify one canonical reshare transcript before committing; reject any cross-epoch material; verify new shares against the unchanged group public key before deleting old shares.
attacks.residualRisk: Nostr relays provide no ordering or consensus; building reliable authenticated resharing on them is the same load-bearing-liveness problem, and proactive refresh only bounds, not eliminates, mobile-adversary risk.

attacks.name: Quorum-offline expiry coercion (timelock-boundary liveness DoS)
attacks.description: Read a pool's T_exp ladder from public kind-38400/38402 events (funding heights are on-chain and announced). In the ~1008-block window before deadlines cluster, knock 3 of 5 operators offline at once: L4-DDoS their paid relays and signing endpoints, BGP/route-leak their ASNs, or serve abuse/legal takedowns to relay hosts. With fewer than k signers, no rounds, refreshes, arkoor cosigns, or sweeps occur (exit-only mode). Every holder must unilaterally exit on-chain simultaneously, precisely when fee pressure peaks. Sustaining the outage across the refresh margin converts a temporary halt into pool-wide forced exit.
attacks.mitigation: Geographically/AS-diverse operators behind hidden services; n much larger than k (e.g., 3-of-9); keep the existing ~7-day refresh margin generous; watchtower auto-exit before expiry; per-operator heartbeat (kind 31401) so clients pre-emptively exit on detected degradation rather than at the cliff.
attacks.residualRisk: A funded adversary can still force pool-wide exit by sustaining a multi-operator outage across the margin; theft is impossible but liveness and fee predictability are not.

attacks.name: Refresh-ceremony griefing (Sybil-seat + branch-stall collapse)
attacks.description: Receiving arkoor is free and needs no on-chain setup (R4), so accrue hundreds of dust vTXOs to distinct keys across many branches — each a penalty-immune 'existing holder' seat satisfying the forfeitable-ownership intent gate. Join every hourly round, complete MuSig2 round 1, then withhold the round-2 partial just inside the 30s timer. Branch-only signing shares nodes, so one withholder stalls everyone on that radix-4 branch; the <=3 re-proposals then fail the round. Over lossy relays, withholding is indistinguishable from packet loss, so per-vTXO penalization cannot fire. Repeat hourly; legitimate refreshers miss windows and cascade into delegated/forced exit.
attacks.mitigation: Non-dust seat minimum plus escalating per-vTXO PoW; a forfeitable fee bonded at intent that is slashed on non-completion (not only on proven equivocation); randomized/segregated branches so one staller can't block disjoint refreshers; longer phase timers; reputation-weighted seat allocation.
attacks.residualRisk: Malice is indistinguishable from genuine relay loss, so honest users get penalized or the griefer escapes; cost-to-grief stays far below cost-to-defend.

attacks.name: Exit-storm fee spike strands sub-economic vTXOs
attacks.description: Trigger a correlated exit (via the quorum DoS, or just DDoS the quorum) so a pool's holders broadcast inside one fee window. Each exit needs depth-5 node txs plus a leaf claim plus a P2A CPFP child (~2.2 kvB first-mover), and every tx must pay fees through the keyless anchor. Simultaneously fee-snipe L1 with high-fee filler to push the floor to 50-100 sat/vB. A 10k-sat vTXO now costs more than its value to exit; rational holders abandon it and the quorum sweeps the residue at T_exp. Laddered expiries don't help once the adversary forces the timing.
attacks.mitigation: Wallet value-at-risk cap that consolidates dust before deadlines; batch exits across shared branches; pre-emptive off-peak exits driven by fee-rate oracles; minimum vTXO denomination so leaves stay exit-economical; operator-subsidized emergency exit batching at mass-exit.
attacks.residualRisk: Any vTXO whose value approaches its ~450 vB-2.2 kvB exit cost is economically strandable on demand; dust holders predictably lose their leaves to the expiry sweep.

attacks.name: TRUC anchor-slot contention / CPFP fee-escalation grief
attacks.description: Exit packages are nVersion=3 (TRUC): a parent admits at most one unconfirmed child, and the keyless P2A anchor is spendable by anyone. During a storm, attach your own minimal-fee child to a victim's (or a shared branch's) node-tx anchor first, occupying the single child slot. The honest CPFP must RBF-replace your child, paying strictly more; you re-pin just below each time, forcing a fee-escalation war that delays confirmation of the shared branch and every exit beneath it. Shared-branch node txs amplify this: one contested parent stalls all descendant exits.
attacks.mitigation: Have the legitimate exiter pre-sign its own minimum-feerate child at creation so the anchor isn't a free slot; submit 1p1c via submitpackage so the child is evaluated atomically; mempool policy favoring higher-feerate children; SIGHASH_ANYONECANPAY fee contributions instead of a shared anchor.
attacks.residualRisk: Attacker can still push defenders into higher fees and delayed confirmation during congestion; griefing remains cheap relative to the delay imposed on shared branches.

attacks.name: Data-availability stranding of arkoor funds defeats seed-only recovery
attacks.description: Arkoor-received value never touches L1, so its exit data (full tx chain + sigs in the 1059->24406 gift wrap) is discoverable ONLY from relay copies plus Q's archive — not from seed-derived L1 scanning. Relays guarantee no storage and routinely purge; accelerate eviction by flooding the victim's read relays with high-volume events to pressure retention/LRU, then DDoS or legally pressure operator archives. An offline receiver returns to find no gift wrap anywhere and cannot reconstruct the spend path. The grafted CLTV recovery-leaf cannot save these funds: the current off-chain owner's UTXO is not on-chain and not seed-derivable.
attacks.mitigation: Mandatory client-side persistent backup of every received package; receiver-side replication-verified finality (don't show received until confirmed on >=k independent mirrors); paid pinning subscriptions with audited retention SLAs; force a prompt on-chain checkpoint of received arkoor above a low threshold so funds become L1-recoverable.
attacks.residualRisk: Received arkoor value held by a long-offline user stays strandable via coordinated purge plus archive denial; seed-only recovery of off-chain receipts is structurally impossible.

attacks.name: NIP-65 relay-set eclipse hides conflicts and refresh windows
attacks.description: Read the victim's read relays from their public kind-10002, then deny an honest view: L4-DDoS or TCP-reset those relays, or (if you can replace their 10002 via key reuse, a compromised client, or an accepted malicious relay recommendation) repoint them to attacker-friendly relays. The receive flow's 'check 38403 on >=3 independent relays' is then satisfied entirely by attacker relays showing no conflict; round announcements (38401) are withheld so the victim never sees refresh windows. Result: the victim is stranded past the T_exp-1008 deadline and simultaneously exposed in the offline-receive double-spend window.
attacks.mitigation: Hard-code a diverse bootstrap relay set independent of operator curation; require attestations from relays under distinct operators/ASNs with signed relay identity; Tor over multiple independent circuits; client alarms on stale round-announcement gaps; cross-check L1 round txids against explorer/compact-filter ground truth.
attacks.residualRisk: A network-position adversary (ISP, hostile Wi-Fi, state) can still partition a target's reachable relays; 'independence' is unverifiable from the client's vantage point.

attacks.name: Sweep-at-expiry confiscation of offline or censored users
attacks.description: The round's CLTV path `<T_exp> CLTV DROP <Q> CHECKSIG` lets a live quorum sweep everything after expiry. A user offline past T_exp-720 who never filed a watch request (a never-yet-online arkoor receiver cannot file one), or whose 38404 watch-request and pre-deposit events were dropped by censoring relays, gets no tower broadcast. Combine: censor the victim's watch requests (relay eclipse) and let the legitimate quorum reach T_exp; Q sweeps the unexited leaf. Funds move to the operator by protocol, not theft — pure liveness/censorship-induced confiscation of a passive holder.
attacks.mitigation: Default automatic watchtower height-deposits funded at receipt for every vTXO; multiple independent towers per leaf; operator-run backstop towers with published SLAs; a consensus recovery tapleaf paying the owner after expiry instead of a Q-only sweep; client refuses receipt without a confirmed tower commitment.
attacks.residualRisk: The watchtower market is thin and censorable; offline users beyond the margin with suppressed watch requests still lose leaves to the expiry sweep.

attacks.name: Refresh hash-lock atomicity freeze (preimage withholding)
attacks.description: Refresh consumes the user's old vTXO as an input to the new round tx; activating the new leaf gates on a preimage Q reveals only after that round tx confirms — and the reveal is a censorable Nostr event. A colluding quorum subset lets the round tx confirm (old vTXO now spent on-chain) then withholds/censors the preimage. The user now has no activated new leaf and no spendable old vTXO; the script-level atomicity is asserted, not specified, so there may be no unilateral path to force the preimage. Balances freeze until reveal — indefinitely under sustained censorship.
attacks.mitigation: Specify the forfeit/new-leaf swap as an on-chain atomic PTLC where the same preimage that lets Q claim the forfeit lets the user claim the new leaf; publish the preimage to >=8 relays with replication proof; add a timeout path returning the old vTXO if the reveal is late.
attacks.residualRisk: Until atomicity is script-enforced and proven, a colluding quorum can freeze mid-refresh balances by withholding an off-chain reveal; only fraud-proof accountability, not recovery, remains.

attacks.name: Coordination-event censorship strands receive-finality and refresh discovery
attacks.description: The 38403 cosign log and quorum no-conflict attestation must be seen before a receiver treats funds as safe, and 38400/38401 announce pools and round phase deadlines. A relay-level adversary selectively drops these to a target (no fund movement needed): the receiver is pinned in permanent 'uncheckpointed' limbo and cannot safely spend, and the holder never learns refresh windows so misses the deadline ladder. Because operators curate the per-pool relay set (>=2 operator-run), they can stack it so the victim lacks 3 genuinely independent honest relays.
attacks.mitigation: Receiver requires attestations from operator-independent relays/ASNs and falls back to direct L1 verification; clients ignore operator-supplied relay curation and use a diverse pinned set; signed monotonic sequence (kind 30178) with inclusion proofs so a withheld latest entry is detectable; timeout-to-exit if attestations stall.
attacks.residualRisk: Targeted, low-detectability withholding keeps a specific user perpetually unfinalized or deadline-blind, without ever being provable as an attack.

attacks.name: Anti-spam gate (PoW + paid AUTH) as a censorship/liveness chokepoint
attacks.description: Intents need NIP-13 PoW >=20 bits plus paid writes and NIP-42 AUTH. Two abuses: (a) flood the pool relays so they raise minimum PoW under load — low-power mobile clients cannot mine an intent within the 30s phase timer and silently drop out of refresh near deadlines; (b) operator-run paid relays selectively deny AUTH or stall writes for a targeted npub, a deniable per-user censorship lever that blocks that user's refresh intents and exit/watch events while serving everyone else.
attacks.mitigation: Allow intent submission across many independent relays so one AUTH denial isn't fatal; cap/standardize PoW so it cannot be inflated against mobile; pre-mine PoW ahead of the window; signed proof-of-write receipts so AUTH denial is attributable; keep a non-paid public-relay fallback path.
attacks.residualRisk: A relay can always slow or deny a specific identity deniably; PoW inherently disadvantages the mobile users the protocol targets, exactly during congestion.

attacks.name: Boarding-deposit strand via post-broadcast quorum stall
attacks.description: Boarding funds an on-chain P2TR 2-of-2 (U,Q) whose only unilateral escape is the `4320 CSV <U>` refund (~30 days). Watch the chain for boarding txs (their address template is recognizable) and time a quorum DoS to the moment after a victim's boarding tx confirms but before it is converted into a round leaf. The deposit is now locked in 2-of-2 with an uncooperative quorum; the victim's sole exit is to wait the full 30-day CSV. Repeated against new entrants, this denies onboarding and strands fresh capital at will.
attacks.mitigation: Shorter boarding refund CSV (a few days) traded off against conversion latency; give a pre-signed unilateral timeout reclaim tx at deposit; convert boarding into a leaf in the same round it confirms; warn users not to board during degraded-quorum heartbeats.
attacks.residualRisk: Any deposit caught between confirmation and conversion is strandable for the full refund CSV; onboarding is a reliable DoS target around quorum outages.

attacks.name: Blossom-hosted tree-commitment data-availability loss
attacks.description: Round results (38402) may store the 1024-leaf vTXO-tree commitment off-relay as a Blossom sha256 blob to keep events small. Blossom servers carry weaker availability guarantees than relays and are a narrow target: DDoS or simply wait out retention on the one or two referenced hosts. Without the tree commitment, a returning user cannot reconstruct cosigner sets and node-tx templates to assemble their root-to-leaf exit path, even though vault and keys are intact — the missing piece is exit data, not keys.
attacks.mitigation: Inline tree commitments in the event, or replicate the Blossom blob across many independent content-addressed mirrors; clients persist the full path locally at signing time; require >=k-mirror replication proof before treating a round as final; reconstruct templates deterministically from seed where possible.
attacks.residualRisk: Any exit path depending on a fetched external commitment is strandable by taking down a small mirror set; local persistence is the only real defense.

attacks.name: Decrementing-locktime graft creates an exhaustible exit window
attacks.description: The grafted decrementing absolute-locktime staleness ordering gives each successive exit/claim package an earlier locktime so the rightful owner's exit matures first. But the budget is finite: forcing rapid refresh churn (via ceremony griefing) or maximal arkoor chaining burns down the locktime headroom. As packages approach the floor, successive owners' exits crowd into a shrinking validity window or collide, and very stale-but-legitimate exits can fall outside any valid range, becoming unbroadcastable until a later height — re-introducing the very race the graft was meant to remove.
attacks.mitigation: Size the locktime ladder with large headroom versus the maximum plausible refresh/arkoor frequency; reset the decrement budget at each on-chain checkpoint; keep arkoor hops capped (already 4) and rate-limit refreshes per epoch; surface remaining headroom in-wallet and force a checkpoint before exhaustion.
attacks.residualRisk: High-churn vTXOs can still approach locktime exhaustion, narrowing or invalidating exit windows under sustained forced-refresh pressure.

attacks.name: vHTLC swap stalls and replacement-cycling strand bridge funds
attacks.description: LN gateway and cross-pool transfers use vHTLCs with a 144-block CLTV delta; the design admits replacement-cycling-class mempool games apply here. As counterparty (or a third party flooding the mempool), replacement-cycle the HTLC-spending tx around the timeout boundary so neither claim nor refund confirms when expected, locking both user and gateway funds for the full CLTV and beyond. For cross-pool swaps between two quorums, stalling one quorum mid-swap locks the in-flight value in the HTLC until timeout, blocking interop liveness.
attacks.mitigation: Aggressive rebroadcast and fee-bumping of HTLC claims; shorten and randomize CLTV deltas; prefer PTLC/adaptor constructions less exposed to preimage-replacement games; gateway liquidity buffers and fail-safe-to-refund timeouts; monitor both legs across independent relays.
attacks.residualRisk: Replacement cycling is mitigated, not eliminated; swap and cross-pool funds remain temporarily lockable for the CLTV window by a determined mempool adversary.

attacks.name: Single-aborter round-collapse griefing (free, hourly)
attacks.description: The root output spend must be signed by MuSig2-agg of ALL round participants, so the tree cannot safely finalize unless every cosigner completes. Hold several cheaply-boarded vTXOs; submit valid 24400 intents (20-bit PoW is ~1M hashes, trivial on a GPU); complete the pubnonce phase; then withhold partial sigs or send garbage. One withholder blocks the root tx for the entire <=1024-user round. Aborting forfeits nothing (forfeit only binds after the new round confirms), so the same vTXOs grief every hour for free. With ~4 intents you exhaust the <=3 re-proposal limit and kill each round, freezing all refreshes and stranding balances as uncheckpointed until forced on-chain exit.
attacks.mitigation: Require a slashable bond posted before the nonce phase, forfeited on abort-after-nonce; finalize the participant set after nonce submission and rebuild excluding non-responders within the same attempt; raise PoW and add per-vTXO and per-key intent rate limits; reputation-gate. None fully remove the free-abort incentive without real collateral slashing.
attacks.residualRisk: Bonds add UX friction and capital cost; adversaries split across many keys/vTXOs to stay under per-key caps; some honest aborts still disrupt rounds.

attacks.name: Operator liquidity amplification via refresh churn
attacks.description: Each refresh moves a vTXO into a new round whose outputs Q funds on-chain; Q recovers the matching old-round capital only at that round's T_exp (~30 days). Repeatedly board then refresh a balance hourly: every refresh strands a fresh tranche of Q's fronted capital for 30 days, so steady-state locked float approx balance x refreshes-in-30-days (up to ~720x). Refresh fees (~0.38%/refresh) total a few hundred percent of your small balance to immobilize hundreds of times that in operator capital, leverage of order 100-250x. Run from multiple keys to drain the ~10 BTC/10k-user float, halting honest refreshes and boarding.
attacks.mitigation: Price refresh fees on capital-lock duration, not remaining lifetime; impose per-identity refresh-rate limits and a minimum dwell time between refreshes; surcharge rapid re-refresh; cap outstanding fronted capital per key; recycle connectors to shorten locks. The carrying cost is structurally Ark's.
attacks.residualRisk: Adversary spreads across keys/pools to evade caps; honest high-velocity users hit the same limits, degrading UX; structural capital cost remains.

attacks.name: Operator as global payment-graph surveillance point
attacks.description: Operators are a passive adversary with identities. At each arkoor cosign Q sees the spent vTXO, both new outputs, the one-time key P_B, and the amount. When the receiver later refreshes P_B, the 24400 intent carries a vTXO ownership proof Q verifies, binding P_B to the receiver's key; boarding ties keys to on-chain identity. Any single one of the five 'independent' operators thus reconstructs the entire payment graph: senders, receivers, amounts, balances, timing, chained hops. The one-time key only hides the npub from relays, never from Q. This is strictly worse than Lightning, where no single party observes the whole graph.
attacks.mitigation: Blind the cosign so Q signs without learning amount or linkage (blind Schnorr/credential schemes), or use Chaumian-ecash-style blinded issuance for arkoor; separate refresh ownership proofs from spend identity; rotate receiver keys per payment; minimize operator-visible metadata. Hard to reconcile with Q's double-spend log.
attacks.residualRisk: Double-spend prevention inherently needs Q to relate spends; blinding adds heavy crypto and may weaken portable fraud proofs; full graph privacy likely unattainable here.

attacks.name: Public amount-revealing payment DAG in 38403
attacks.description: The 38403 cosign log is public and, per arkoor, names the spent vTXO, the resulting payment output P_B, the change output, the sequence number, and the amount. Anyone scraping relays reconstructs the complete vTXO-level payment DAG with amounts and timing. Change-detection heuristics (the output reused by the sender's next arkoor) separate payer change from payee output; chained arkoor (<=4 hops) is fully linked. Deanonymizing any single node, via a refresh, a gateway swap touching Lightning/L1, or an exit to a known address, collapses the whole connected component to real identities and exposes balances.
attacks.mitigation: Publish only commitments/nullifiers rather than cleartext outputs and amounts; hide amounts with range proofs; avoid deterministic change linkage; shorten retention; let receivers verify via private inclusion proofs (design-C Merkle commitments) instead of a public flat log.
attacks.residualRisk: Timing and tree-structure metadata still leak; commitments must still let Q detect double-spends; gateway and exit endpoints remain deanonymization anchors.

attacks.name: Stealth one-time key reuse (missing per-payment nonce)
attacks.description: The stealth derivation P_B = B + H(ECDH(a,B))*G has no per-payment tweak. For a fixed sender key a and receiver key B the shared secret is constant, so every payment A->B yields the identical one-time key P_B and identical leaf scriptpubkey. Repeated payments between the same pair are trivially linkable in the public 38403 log and on-chain at exit, and the address reuse degrades the receiver's privacy. An adversary suspecting a relationship confirms it by spotting the repeated P_B across log entries.
attacks.mitigation: Include a per-output nonce in the hash: P_B = B + H(ECDH(a,B) || outpoint or counter)*G, as in BIP-47/Silent Payments, so each payment derives a fresh unlinkable key and never reuses a scriptpubkey.
attacks.residualRisk: Receiver must scan a counter space or use Silent-Payments-style tweaks; sender bookkeeping needed; correct implementation required to avoid accidental reuse.

attacks.name: Recipient leak via NIP-65 delivery relays
attacks.description: Gift wraps are delivered to 'Bob's NIP-65 read relays' resolved from his public kind-10002. The p-tag one-time key hides Bob's npub inside the event, but the delivery destination does not: any relay receiving a kind-1059 wrap knows it belongs to the owner of that read-relay set, i.e. Bob. Few or colluding relays, or an operator running relays, map wrap -> relay-set fingerprint -> npub, and correlate inbound wrap timing with Bob's subsequent online activity (a 24400 intent from the same relay set), reconstructing who-paid-whom without breaking any encryption.
attacks.mitigation: Use large shared/anonymity-set relays not uniquely tied to one npub; deliver via mix or blinded routing or to randomized relay subsets; add padding and decoy traffic; access over Tor; decouple receive relays from the publicly advertised 10002.
attacks.residualRisk: Anonymity set bounded by shared-relay popularity; decoys cost bandwidth; global relay observers and timing correlation still narrow the recipient.

attacks.name: Replacement-cycling / TRUC child-slot grief on exits
attacks.description: Exit txs are zero-fee TRUC v3 with an anyone-can-spend P2A anchor, requiring CPFP, and TRUC permits only one unconfirmed child. Spend the anchor with a low-feerate child that also spends a watchtower/user-funded input, occupying the single child slot without confirming the parent. When the honest party RBFs your child, broadcast a conflicting tx spending the shared funded input elsewhere at higher fee, evicting their replacement (replacement cycling) and dropping the parent back to childless/zero-fee. Repeat each block near the 144-block CSV or T_exp deadline so the exit never confirms in time; the operator then sweeps.
attacks.mitigation: Fund CPFP children only from dedicated anchor-spend UTXOs the adversary cannot conflict; exploit TRUC's bounded child size with aggressive rebroadcast and out-of-band miner submission; keep deadline buffers (the 1008-block margin); have multiple independent watchtowers race bumps.
attacks.residualRisk: Replacement cycling is unsolved at consensus level; fee spikes plus cycling can still delay confirmation past deadlines; watchtower funding adds cost and attack surface.

attacks.name: Targeted fee-spike timing on T_exp deadlines
attacks.description: Pool T_exp ladders are published in 38400 and each round's funding height is on-chain, so every pool's T_exp-720 watchtower-broadcast window is publicly computable. A well-funded adversary floods the mempool with high-fee transactions during a target pool's exit window, pushing feerates above the level at which sub-10k-sat vTXOs are economical to exit and above fixed watch-request bounties. Exits stall; at T_exp the operator legitimately sweeps the expired round, confiscating small holders. Laddering only forces the adversary to attack rungs sequentially, which a funded actor sustains across the month.
attacks.mitigation: Use dynamic, fee-rate-indexed watch bounties and user fee reserves; lengthen pre-expiry margins; graft the recovery tapleaf so dormant funds degrade to self-custody instead of being swept; consolidate dust before expiry; randomize deadlines further.
attacks.residualRisk: Sustained fee pressure still strands dust-sized vTXOs; recovery tapleaf depends on being grafted and on locktime maturity; users pay elevated exit fees regardless.

attacks.name: Dust vTXO flooding of leaf slots and cosign log
attacks.description: Arkoor self-payments split one vTXO into payment+change for ~1-3 sats + 0.05%, both new vTXOs. Cheaply generate thousands of dust vTXOs, then submit a refresh intent per dust vTXO; each is a valid forfeitable-ownership proof that satisfies the anti-grief gate. Each round has only <=1024 leaf slots, so flooding intents starves honest refreshers of slots, while the per-vTXO 38403 sequence entries plus Q's archive bloat unboundedly, raising relay storage and client scan costs. Honest users unable to refresh drift into forced on-chain exits.
attacks.mitigation: Enforce a minimum vTXO/leaf value (anti-dust floor); per-identity slot quotas per round; a fixed sats floor on refresh fees so dust is uneconomical; prune the log to active vTXOs; charge for log/archive retention.
attacks.residualRisk: Adversary spreads dust across keys to evade quotas; anti-dust floors hurt legitimate micropayments; log growth still burdens relays during an attack.

attacks.name: Gift-wrap spam flood on receiver relays
attacks.description: Anyone can publish kind-1059 events to a victim's publicly known read relays. Flood those relays with millions of well-formed but bogus gift wraps p-tagged to random one-time keys. On waking, the receiver cannot distinguish real payments without NIP-44 trial-decrypting every wrap, draining battery, bandwidth, and time, and burying the genuine arkoor package. A merchant or offline user may miss a real payment's refresh deadline, pushing trusted funds toward T_exp risk. PoW and paid-write defenses are absent on the public relays the receiver must read.
attacks.mitigation: Require PoW or paid-write on receive relays; rate-limit per relay; have the sender include a cheap pre-auth tag the receiver filters before decrypting; subscribe to curated relays; client-side dedup and prioritization.
attacks.residualRisk: PoW raises legitimate sender cost and battery use; determined adversaries still pay PoW at scale; curated relays reduce censorship resistance and shrink the anonymity set.

attacks.name: Targeted relay-eviction to force expensive exits
attacks.description: A victim's read relays are public (kind-10002) and the pool relay set is in 38400. DoS or rate-limit precisely those relays during round windows so the victim's 24400 intents and 24402/24403 signing messages arrive after the 30-second phase timers. The coordinator evicts the 'unresponsive' victim every round, so they can never checkpoint a received arkoor balance. They are forced into a unilateral on-chain exit (4.5k-22k sats) or, if offline, risk the expiry sweep. A cheap targeted Nostr-layer latency attack converts directly into the victim's on-chain cost.
attacks.mitigation: Use many redundant, geographically diverse relays; adaptive phase timers with grace for late-but-valid messages; let users publish through fresh relays not tied to the public 10002; detect targeted relay outages and reschedule the victim into a later round.
attacks.residualRisk: Generous timers slow rounds for everyone and widen the abort-grief window; adversaries can DoS even large relay sets for one high-value target.

attacks.name: Operator/paid-relay censorship of watch requests and alerts
attacks.description: Operators run >=2 of the >=8 relays and know each victim's relay set (public 10002 + 38400). For a known-offline arkoor receiver, selectively drop that victim's 38404 watch request and any 38405 watchtower alerts on the relays they control, and pressure or DoS the rest, so no watchtower broadcasts the exit before T_exp-720. At T_exp the operators legitimately sweep the expired round, capturing funds the offline user could not defend. The thin, operator-dominated watchtower market means operator-run towers may be the only ones watching, closing the loop into theft-by-censorship within the stated trust window.
attacks.mitigation: Mandate redundant independent watchtowers and height-deposit pre-broadcast (graft) so exits fire without live alerts; user-side multi-relay publication with delivery confirmation; recovery tapleaf so dormant funds are not swept; slashing and signed-deletion attestations for misbehaving operators.
attacks.residualRisk: Offline users still depend on at least one honest funded watchtower receiving the request; operator tower monoculture plus relay collusion keep a censorship-to-sweep path open.

attacks.name: vHTLC gateway liquidity exhaustion (free option)
attacks.description: vHTLC LN swaps lock gateway Lightning liquidity for the 144-block CLTV delta. As initiator, open many swaps that commit the gateway's inbound/outbound HTLC capacity, then delay or never reveal the preimage (free-option / hold griefing). The gateway's capital sits frozen for the CLTV window per swap; running many concurrently exhausts its liquidity, blocking honest LN bridging and degrading the day-one interop story. Repeat across gateways. Attacker cost is minimal since aborted swaps cost only fees, not principal.
attacks.mitigation: Charge non-refundable upfront swap reservation fees; cap concurrent in-flight value per identity; use short CLTV deltas; require hold-invoice-style penalties; demand collateral or reputation for large swaps; diversify across many gateways.
attacks.residualRisk: Upfront fees deter casual but not well-funded attackers; short CLTVs raise honest-failure risk; a thin gateway market means few targets to saturate.

attacks.name: Wallet vault (37400) metadata leakage
attacks.description: The 37400 wallet vault is an addressable event authored by the user's main npub. Although content is NIP-44 self-encrypted, the event's author, existence, ciphertext size, and update timestamps are public. An observer watches a target npub's vault: growing size implies more vTXOs and longer arkoor history (accumulating wealth); frequent updates imply active spending or receiving. This yields a per-npub wealth-and-activity estimator without decrypting anything, tied directly to the user's identity.
attacks.mitigation: Author the vault under a per-user derived key unlinkable to the main npub (deterministic from seed for recovery); pad ciphertext to fixed-size buckets; batch and randomize update timing; split across decoy events.
attacks.residualRisk: Padding and decoys cost storage/bandwidth; coarse buckets still leak order-of-magnitude wealth; update cadence under load may still correlate with activity.

attacks.name: Watchtower watch-request deanonymization harvesting
attacks.description: Watchtowers are permissionless and 38404 watch requests carry the exit package: the vTXO path txs (amount, tree position) and the pre-signed claim paying the user's BIP-86 L1 address, plus deadline and bounty. If public, this is open deanonymization; if 'encrypted to chosen watchtowers,' the chosen tower still learns it. Run many attractive (high-bounty, reliable) watchtowers to harvest these requests at scale, building a database mapping vTXO <-> on-chain L1 address <-> amount <-> (via the public payment graph and refresh timing) npub. This links Nostr identities to concrete Bitcoin addresses and balances.
attacks.mitigation: Encrypt watch requests to freshly derived per-request keys; split the exit package across multiple towers so none sees the full mapping; use blinded or threshold watch schemes; do not embed the final L1 address, derive it only at claim time.
attacks.residualRisk: Colluding towers recombine shards; the broadcasting tower necessarily learns the on-chain footprint at exit; a thin tower market concentrates harvested data.

# Flock v0.2 — Federated Ark over Nostr (Consolidated Architecture)

## 1. Executive summary

Flock is a Bitcoin Layer-2 successor to Lightning: covenant-less Ark pools operated by a k-of-n FROST quorum, with **all** off-chain coordination, state backup, and watchtower traffic carried as Nostr events over untrusted public relays. Users receive instantly to an npub with zero on-chain setup, no channels, and no liquidity management; the capital burden moves to operators and is explicitly priced. v0.2 eliminates the contest's worst flaw: the unproven FROST-inside-MuSig2 composition is **removed** — every quorum-gated output now uses a tapscript requiring two independent BIP-340 signatures, so Q signs only plain FROST-Schnorr (RFC 9591 / FROSTR-class, shipped) and MuSig2 runs only among user cohorts with CSPRNG nonces. Refresh atomicity is rebuilt on Ark-style **connector outputs** (transaction-graph binding) instead of asserted hash-locks. Stale-exit defense becomes a Spark-precedented **decrementing relative-timelock claim ladder** — race-free and valid even under a dead quorum — replacing the reactive 144-block contest. A rotating **CLTV recovery tapleaf** lets dormant funds degrade to plain self-custody instead of being swept at expiry, and enables seed-only recovery once a tree is unrolled. Round liveness is restructured: one 1024-cosigner ceremony becomes 16 independent 64-leaf **cells** with post-nonce participant finalization and forfeitable intent bonds, so one aborter delays one cell by one attempt. The trust-downgraded delegated refresh is **deleted**; offline users are protected by sender-funded watchtower height-deposits plus the recovery leaf. Residual trust is explicit and bounded: uncheckpointed arkoor receipts are trusted (sender plus k-of-n collusion) until the next checkpoint, capped by a wallet value-at-risk policy; checkpointed funds are theft-proof with unilateral exit. Open problems are conceded, not glossed: operator payment-graph visibility, data availability of uncheckpointed receipts, mempool replacement cycling, and a structural ~0.3–0.5%/month carrying cost on actively refreshed balances.

## 2. Architecture

**Roles.**
- **Operators O1..O7** (independent orgs, diverse ASNs/jurisdictions, hidden services): hold FROST shares of group key **Q** (k=4 of n=7 — theft needs 4 colluding, liveness survives 3 down). PedPoP DKG at genesis; monthly proactive resharing over signed, epoch-tagged transcripts.
- **Relays** (≥8 per pool, ≥3 mandated operator-independent): untrusted transport and best-effort storage. Clients additionally use a hard-coded diverse bootstrap set.
- **Wallets**: hold a seed → Nostr key + Bitcoin xprv; otherwise stateless (vault-recoverable). Enforce value-at-risk and finality policies client-side.
- **Watchtowers**: permissionless, keyless; execute height-deposits ("broadcast package P at height H unless superseded") and CPFP via P2A.
- **LN gateways**: vHTLC/PTLC swap providers; existing LSPs can pivot here with the same capital and no per-edge lockup (LSP migration path for R1).

```
                          BITCOIN L1
   round tx (hourly/pool: 16 cell roots + connectors)   forfeits/claims/sweeps
            ▲                                   ▲
            │   FROST 4-of-7 quorum Q — plain BIP-340 sigs only
            └───────────────┬───────────────────┘
                            │ ALL traffic = Nostr events
 ┌──────────────────────────┴───────────────────────────────────┐
 │  PUBLIC NOSTR RELAYS (untrusted; ≥8/pool, ≥3 non-operator)   │
 │  pool ads · cell ceremonies · arkoor gift wraps · Merkle     │
 │  checkpoint log · vaults · height-deposits · gateway offers  │
 └──┬───────────────┬──────────────────┬───────────────┬────────┘
  Alice           Bob (OFFLINE        Watchtowers     LN Gateways
  (sender)        receiver: npub only) (keyless CPFP + (vHTLC ↔ BOLT11/12)
                                       height-deposits)
```

A pool's hourly **round tx** funds 16 independent 64-leaf pre-signed trees ("cells", radix-4, depth 3) expiring at **T_exp = funding height + 4320 (~30 d)**. Payments are out-of-round (**arkoor**) cosigns: instant, no receiver liveness, no per-payment operator capital. Rounds serve only refreshes/boarding (senders = receivers).

## 3. On-chain construction

All quorum-gated spends use script paths with **two separate signatures** (`<X> OP_CHECKSIGVERIFY <Q> OP_CHECKSIG`): users/cohorts sign standard MuSig2 or single-key Schnorr; Q signs the same digest independently via plain FROST. No nonce coupling between the two protocols exists anywhere.

**Round tx** (per pool per hour; inputs: Q capital + boarding outputs + forfeited value): outputs = 16 **cell roots**, per-user **connector outputs** (dust-sized, one per refreshing user), Q change.

**Cell root / node outputs**: internal key = NUMS (unspendable). Tapscripts: (a) *tree path*: `<AggU_branch> CHECKSIGVERIFY <Q> CHECKSIG` where AggU = MuSig2 aggregate of the users below that branch (each user cosigns only their root-to-leaf path, depth 3, then deletes the ephemeral key — their own deletion binds the pseudo-covenant); (b) *node sweep*: `<T_exp+4032> CLTV DROP <Q> CHECKSIG` (late garbage collection only).

**vTXO leaf output**: NUMS internal key. Tapscripts: (a) *cooperative*: `<U> CHECKSIGVERIFY <Q> CHECKSIG` — used for arkoor, forfeits, offboards, and pre-signing claims; (b) *recovery leaf*: `<T_exp+288> CLTV DROP <U_ckpt> CHECKSIG` paying the **checkpointed** owner's seed-derivable key — dormancy degrades to self-custody; (c) *leaf sweep*: `<T_exp+4032> CLTV DROP <Q> CHECKSIG`. There is **no** bare CSV exit script (it would let stale owners bypass the ladder).

**Claim ladder (replaces the 144-CSV contest).** Every owner holds a pre-signed *claim tx* spending the leaf's cooperative path to their own key, with consensus-enforced BIP-68 nSequence: checkpointed owner (hop 0) nSequence = 720; each arkoor hop decrements by 144 (hop 4 = 144; hop cap 4, reset at every checkpoint). The **current owner's claim matures strictly before any prior owner's** once the leaf is on-chain — no mempool race, no live quorum needed. Q cosigns the claim atomically with each arkoor transfer; a transfer without its claim is invalid and the receiver rejects it.

**Forfeit tx** (refresh atomicity, replaces hash-locks): inputs = old leaf (cooperative path, pre-signed in-ceremony) + a **connector output of the new round tx**. The forfeit is consensus-invalid unless the round tx that actually contains the user's verified new leaf confirms (the connector outpoint commits to that exact txid). Distinct connector per user; no shared preimages; nothing to withhold. Forfeits have nSequence 0, pay Q, and are broadcastable by **anyone** (watchtowers hold copies) — so they beat every laddered claim (min 144) even if Q later dies.

**Boarding output**: `<U> CHECKSIGVERIFY <Q> CHECKSIG` + refund `288 CSV <U>` (~2 days, shortened from 30 — bounds the boarding-strand window); converted in the same round it confirms when possible.

**Fees/pinning**: all tree/claim/forfeit txs are nVersion=3 (TRUC), zero-fee, P2A anchor; the exiter pre-signs its own minimum-feerate child at creation (the anchor is never a free slot) and submits 1p1c via `submitpackage`; CPFP funded from dedicated UTXOs that cannot be conflicted.

**Exit cost** (script-path inputs ≈126 vB): depth-3 unroll = 3 node txs ≈ 321 vB each + claim ≈ 193 vB + CPFP children ≈ 460 vB ⇒ **first exiter ≈ 1.6 kvB (~16k sats @10 sat/vB)**; path already unrolled ⇒ **≈ 310 vB (~3.1k sats)**. Each arkoor hop in an exit chain adds ≈ 235 vB.

**Nonce discipline (load-bearing, corrected):** all MuSig2/FROST round-1 nonces are **CSPRNG-fresh**, RAM-only, never persisted, never re-derived — deterministic session-keyed derivation is banned (it enabled key extraction via induced re-signing). ## 5. Payment flows

**Send (Alice→Bob, ~1–2 s).** Alice derives a per-payment key **P_B = B + H(ECDH(a,B) ‖ round_txid ‖ counter)·G** (per-payment tweak fixes reuse linkage). She builds the arkoor tx (payment vTXO + self-made change), signs cooperatively; Q verifies no nullifier conflict, increments seq, cosigns the transfer **and** the receiver's laddered claim, publishes the 30178 root. Alice gift-wraps the package to Bob's read relays + pool relays, files a funded 38404 height-deposit for Bob (mandatory part of send), and obtains ≥k-relay replication receipts. Proof-of-payment = Merkle inclusion proof under a quorum-signed root.

**Receive while offline.** Bob needs only an npub — no on-chain setup, no liquidity (R4). The wrap waits on relays + Q's archive; the sender-funded height-deposit already protects the funds toward expiry. On waking, Bob: fetches wraps; verifies the sig chain to a confirmed round tx (L1 via compact filters/explorers); fetches 30178 roots from **disjoint relay sets including operator-independent relays, failing closed** on absence; verifies inclusion + replication on ≥k mirrors; persists the package locally. Funds above the **value-at-risk cap (default 50k sats)** are auto-checkpointed at the next round; below it, display as "uncheckpointed" until refreshed. Receives are **refused** against rounds with <2016 blocks to T_exp (sender must refresh first) — bounding the recovery-leaf stale-owner window.

**Refresh / checkpoint (hourly; wallet deadline T_exp − 1008).** Intent (bonded, PoW) → assignment to a 64-leaf cell → verify own leaf/path and the canonical participant-set commitment in the proposal → MuSig2 nonces, then **participant set finalized post-nonce; non-responders excluded and the cell rebuilt in the same attempt** → partials (120 s adaptive phase timers) → sign forfeit spending old leaf + own connector of the proposed round txid → Q broadcasts; confirmation simultaneously activates the new leaf and makes the forfeit valid (connector atomicity — no reveal step to withhold, and a mutated round tx invalidates the forfeit, leaving the old vTXO intact). New leaf: fresh 30-day clock, ladder reset to hop 0, recovery tapleaf rotated to current owner, zero residual trust. Abort-after-nonce slashes the intent bond.

**Unilateral exit.** Broadcast path txs as 1p1c TRUC packages with pre-signed min-fee children; CPFP via P2A (anyone can fund); claim matures after its laddered nSequence (144–720 blocks). No operator cooperation; stale prior owners are consensus-blocked by later locktimes, and live Q (or any tower holding a forfeit) beats refresh-stale leaves immediately.

**Recover from seed alone.** Seed → Nostr key + xprv. Fetch kind-10002 + 37400 vault (derived author key) from bootstrap relays; fall back to Q archives (ciphertext, useless to operators); rebuild vTXO set; cross-check 30178 + L1. If *all* vault copies are gone: checkpointed funds are still recoverable via the **recovery tapleaf** after T_exp+288 once the tree is unrolled (anyone can unroll; Q must unroll to sweep at T_exp+4032, and towers unroll for bounties), using only the seed-derived U_ckpt key. Stale vaults are safe — exiting an already-forfeited leaf only loses an already-spent coin. No toxic state. Conceded: uncheckpointed arkoor receipts are **not** seed-recoverable (§9).

## 6. Trust model and attack analysis

**Explicit residual-trust time bounds.**
- **Uncheckpointed arkoor**: theft requires sender + 4-of-7 operators. Bound: until next checkpoint — auto at next hourly round above 50k sats; hard bound T_exp (receive banned in final 2016 blocks). Equivocation = two signed 30178 roots at one seq: portable fraud proof.
- **Offline safety**: none required until T_exp − 720, when height-deposit towers exit or checkpointed value rides to the recovery leaf (T_exp+288 → self-custody). Worst case for a never-online receiver: tower-dependent until T_exp − 720.
- **Recovery-leaf stale window**: uncheckpointed value whose holder stays offline past T_exp+288 is claimable by the prior checkpointed owner — bounded by the VaR cap and the receive-near-expiry ban.
- **Swaps**: standard HTLC exposure for the 144-block CLTV delta.

## 7. Economics

**Operator model.** Revenue: (1) refresh fees priced on **capital-lock duration** (not remaining lifetime — kills the churn-amplification lever): ~0.3–0.4%/month on refreshed balances against ~5% APY cost of capital; minimum dwell time and per-leaf rate limits cap fronted-capital leverage; (2) arkoor cosign fees 1–3 sats + 0.05% (near-pure margin); (3) gateway swap fees 0.1–0.5%; (4) paid relay/vault pinning subscriptions (~1–2k sats/mo). A 10k-user pool at 100k-sat average needs ~10 BTC recycling float — honest framing: a capital-intensive LSP-like business; existing Lightning LSPs can migrate with the same balance sheet and better capital efficiency (no per-edge lockup).

**User costs.** Receive: free. Send: 1–3 sats + 0.05%. Hot (refreshed) balances: ~0.3–0.4%/month. **Dormant balances: zero** — skip refreshes entirely, degrade to self-custody via the recovery leaf; no forced exit, no monthly-app-open requirement (fixes the flagged carrying-cost/idle-confiscation flaw for savings; the carrying cost now applies only to actively transacted funds, where it substitutes for LN channel/rebalance amortization).

**Exit costs.** First exiter ≈1.6 kvB (~16k sats @10 sat/vB); marginal exiter ≈310 vB (~3.1k sats); +235 vB per arkoor hop (≤4).

**Mass exit.** Per 1024-leaf pool: ~336 node txs + 1024 claims + CPFP ≈ **0.33 blocks (~310 vB/user)**; 100k users ≈ ~33 blocks, spread across hourly-laddered T_exp rungs with a 1008-block margin and keyless P2A bumping. Expensive and slow but safe: pre-signed, pinning-hardened, counterparty-free, and ladder-ordered.

## 9. Open problems

1. **Operator payment-graph visibility** — Q necessarily relates spends for double-spend prevention; blinded cosigning compatible with fraud proofs is unsolved. Privacy is below Lightning's.
2. **Uncheckpointed-receipt data availability** — arkoor exit data is not seed-derivable; coordinated relay purge plus archive denial strands long-offline receipts. Structural; bounded only by VaR cap, replication receipts, and auto-checkpointing.
3. **Replacement cycling / fee-spike timing** — no complete mempool-level fix; deadline-adjacent exits can be delayed at cost; defense is margins, dedicated fee UTXOs, and tower redundancy.
4. **Dust** — value near its ~310 vB exit cost is economically strandable; the 10k-sat leaf floor pushes micropayments into uncheckpointed change.
5. **Grief vs. loss indistinguishability** — ceremony withholding cannot be told apart from relay loss; bonds tax honest unlucky users or under-deter attackers.
6. **Accountability without covenants** — operator "slashing" reduces to portable fraud proofs + reputation/legal recourse; on-chain bonds need trusted arbitration.
7. **Structural carrying cost** — ~0.3–0.4%/month on hot balances is intrinsic to covenant-less Ark capital fronting; competitive for payments balances, not for savings (savings go dormant instead).
8. **Recovery-leaf stale window** — sub-cap uncheckpointed value of receivers offline past T_exp+288 is claimable by the prior owner.
9. **Quorum liveness** — <k operators halts new payments and forfeit *creation* (exit-only mode); held forfeits still need a broadcaster within 144 blocks of a stale unroll.
10. **Watchtower market thinness** — height-deposits make action automatic, but a real fee-budgeted tower economy is unproven.

## 10. Future work under covenants

CTV would make tree expansion non-interactive: no MuSig2 ceremonies, no ephemeral-key-deletion assumption, no cells, no aborter griefing — rounds become a single Q broadcast, and offline users refresh trustlessly (Erk-style), deleting open problems 5 and most of 9. CSFS would let leaves verify quorum signatures over *future* state, enabling consensus-enforced forfeit binding, true per-hop recovery-leaf rotation (closing problem 8), and compact rebindable exits. CTV+CSFS together would roughly halve exit vbytes and remove every "someone must broadcast in time" dependency, leaving only the economic and privacy problems. None of this is assumed anywhere above.
